description: Chart selection and design framework. Combines Gene Zelazny's 'Say It With Charts' (message-first chart selection) with Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's 'Storytelling with Data' (visual hierarchy, declutter, strategic attention).
sources: Zelazny, Gene. Say It With Charts. 4th ed. McGraw-Hill.
Knaflic, Cole Nussbaumer. Storytelling with Data. Wiley.

THE_PROCESS.step_1_message: WHAT is the one point this chart makes? Write it as a complete sentence with a verb. This becomes the chart title. If you can't write the sentence, you don't need a chart.
THE_PROCESS.step_2_comparison: WHICH comparison type does your message imply? The message contains trigger words that map to exactly one comparison type. Match them.
THE_PROCESS.step_3_form: WHICH chart form fits that comparison type? The comparison type determines the chart. Not your preference — the data's structure.
THE_PROCESS.step_4_attention: WHERE should the audience look first? Use pre-attentive attributes (color, size, position, boldness) to direct the eye to the ONE thing that matters. Everything else is context — push it to grey.
THE_PROCESS.step_5_declutter: WHAT can be removed? Strip gridlines, borders, redundant labels, legends that repeat the title. Every pixel must earn its place. If removing something doesn't reduce understanding, remove it.

ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.message_pattern: X accounts for Y% of total
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.question: What share of the total does each part represent?
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.chart_form: pie (<=4 slices) or donut (5-6 slices) or stacked_bar (comparison across groups)
rules: Max 6 slices. Group the rest into 'Other'.
Order slices largest to smallest, starting at 12 o'clock.
HIGHLIGHT the one slice that IS the story — bold color. Grey the rest.
Donut center can hold the total number for context.
If comparing composition across 2+ groups (e.g., this year vs last year), use stacked bar — pie can't show change.
anti_patterns: Never use pie for more than 6 items.
Never use pie when the point is ranking — use bar.
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.example_message: Middle East crude accounts for 47% of Jamnagar's intake — the single largest source at risk.

ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.message_pattern: X is larger/smaller than Y by Z
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.question: How do items rank or compare against each other?
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.chart_form: horizontal_bar (always, unless fewer than 4 items — then vertical bar)
rules: Sort bars by value — largest at top. NEVER alphabetical.
The SUBJECT of the message gets a bold color. Everything else is grey.
Show the value label at the end of each bar — the audience reads the number, not the bar length.
Include a reference line if there's a benchmark, average, or threshold.
The GAP between the subject and the comparison is the story — annotate it.
anti_patterns: Never use vertical bars for more than 5 items — labels overlap.
Never use rainbow colors — color encodes meaning, not decoration.
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.example_message: Reliance's NCI of 21.1 is nearly double the next-highest Asian refiner — this is the crude flexibility moat.

ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.message_pattern: X has grown/declined from A to B over period
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.question: How has this changed over time?
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.chart_form: line (>6 periods or continuous trend) or vertical_bar (<=6 discrete periods)
rules: Time ALWAYS goes left to right on the x-axis.
Mark the INFLECTION POINT — the moment the trend changed. That's usually the story.
Add a reference line for targets, thresholds, or danger zones.
Use area fill sparingly — only when the area itself (cumulative volume) is meaningful.
For two series: use solid line for the subject, dashed for the comparison.
Annotate the start value and end value — the delta is the message.
anti_patterns: Never truncate the y-axis to exaggerate a trend — start at zero unless there's a clear reason.
Never use a line chart for categorical data (countries, products).
Never connect data points that aren't sequential in time.
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.example_message: Brent surged from $78 to $126/bbl in 28 days — the fastest oil price shock since 1990.

ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.message_pattern: Most of X falls in the Y range
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.question: How are items distributed across ranges?
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.chart_form: histogram or bar with range buckets
rules: Group data into meaningful, equal-width ranges.
Highlight the range where the subject sits.
Show the shape — is it normal, skewed, bimodal?
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.example_message: 78% of India's crude imports transit Hormuz — concentration risk in a single chokepoint.

ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.message_pattern: As X increases, Y also increases/decreases
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.question: Is there a relationship between two variables?
rules: Label both axes clearly with units.
Add a trend line if correlation is strong.
Use bubble size for a third variable if relevant.
HIGHLIGHT the subject as a distinct color/size. Grey the rest.
Divide into quadrants if the story is about positioning (high-high, low-low, etc.).
ZELAZNY_COMPARISON_TYPES.example_message: Refineries with NCI above 12 captured 2-3x the GRM uplift during the 2022 spike — complexity pays in crises.

ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.message_pattern: X starts at A, gains/loses B through several factors, ends at C
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.question: How do parts build up or erode to reach a total?
rules: Start with the base value (blue).
Additions are green, subtractions are red, totals are blue.
Each bar floats from where the previous one ended — this is the whole point.
Label each bar with its value AND what it represents.
Max 7-8 bars. If more, combine small items.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.when_to_use: Margin bridges, cost breakdowns, revenue walks, any time you're explaining HOW you got from point A to point B through contributing factors. This is the most powerful chart type for executive audiences because it answers 'why' not just 'what'.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.example_message: GRM walks from $8/bbl baseline to $14/bbl crisis level: +$3 crude discount, +$4 crack widening, -$1 freight penalty.

ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.message_pattern: X is at Y, which is above/below the Z threshold
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.question: Where does a single KPI stand relative to a target or danger zone?
rules: Color-code zones: green (safe), amber (caution), red (danger).
Show current value LARGE in the center.
Mark the threshold that triggers action.
Use sparingly — only for single critical KPIs, not for comparisons.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.when_to_use: Utilization rates, inventory days cover, capacity limits — any single metric that has a clear 'safe vs danger' threshold.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.example_message: Crude inventory at 14 days cover — below the 18-day safety threshold.

ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.message_pattern: X flows from sources A, B, C to destinations D, E, F
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.question: How does volume flow from origins to destinations?
rules: Width of each flow is proportional to volume.
Color-code by source or by destination — not both.
Label the largest flows. Grey the small ones.
Max 10-12 nodes total or it becomes unreadable.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.when_to_use: Crude sourcing flows, product placement, supply chain routing, revenue by channel → segment.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.example_message: Post-Hormuz crude rerouting: 550 kbd from Middle East drops to 100 kbd; Atlantic Basin rises from 240 to 500 kbd.

ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.message_pattern: Intensity of X varies across dimensions Y and Z
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.question: Where are the hot spots across two categorical dimensions?
rules: Use a single color gradient (light to dark) — NOT rainbow.
Label cells with values if the grid is small enough.
Order rows and columns by total intensity, not alphabetically.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.when_to_use: Scenario matrices, risk heat maps, product-market fit grids, time × category intensity.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.example_message: Crack spread heat map: diesel strongest in Q2 ($28-32/bbl), naphtha weakest year-round.

ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.message_pattern: X narrows from A at the top to B at the bottom through stages
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.question: How much is lost at each stage of a process?
rules: Stages go top to bottom, widest to narrowest.
Label each stage with its value AND the drop-off rate.
Highlight the biggest drop-off — that's the intervention point.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.when_to_use: Conversion funnels, pipeline stages, screening processes.
ADDITIONAL_CHART_TYPES.example_message: Of 50 alternative crude cargoes assessed, only 12 meet quality, logistics, and pricing criteria.

pre_attentive_attributes.principle: The human eye processes color, size, and position BEFORE conscious thought. Use these to direct attention to the ONE thing that matters.
application: BOLD COLOR on the data point that IS the message. GREY everything else.
Larger font/bar for the subject. Smaller for context.
Position the key insight at the visual center or at the end of the eye's natural reading path (top-left to bottom-right).

strategic_color.principle: Color is the most powerful pre-attentive attribute. Use it with intention, never for decoration.

palette.subject_highlight: #2563eb (blue) — the entity or metric you're talking about
palette.context: #94a3b8 (grey) — everything that isn't the story. Most of your chart should be grey.

strategic_color.rule: If more than 2 colors are bold (non-grey), you're not telling a story — you're showing a rainbow. Reduce.

declutter_checklist: Remove gridlines or reduce to very light grey (#f1f5f9).
Remove legend if the chart title or data labels already identify the series.
Remove axis lines if gridlines or data labels convey the scale.
Remove decimal places unless they matter for the argument.
Remove 3D effects, shadows, gradients on bars.
Ask: 'If I remove this element, does the chart still make sense?' If yes, remove it.
KNAFLIC_DESIGN_PRINCIPLES.the_3_second_rule: An executive should understand the chart's message in 3 seconds. If they need to study it, the chart has failed. The title states the conclusion. The visual confirms it. The source provides credibility. Nothing else.

TITLE_RULES.principle: The title IS the message. It is a complete sentence stating what the chart proves. It is NOT a topic label.
good_titles: Diesel cracks surged 55% to $30/bbl — the widest since 2022
Urals delivered $12/bbl cheaper than West African alternatives
PSU refiners face $3-5/bbl margin squeeze at current crude prices
Bypass pipelines cover only 17% of Hormuz's 20 mb/d flow
bad_titles: Crack Spread Comparison (topic label, says nothing)
Crude Price Analysis (what analysis? what conclusion?)
Market Overview (overview of what? so what?)
Refinery Utilization Rates (and? what about them?)

CHART_SELECTION_DECISION_TREE.instruction: Follow this tree IN ORDER. Stop at the first match.

tree.if: Your message is about HOW something builds up or breaks down through contributing factors
tree.why: Waterfalls answer 'why did X change?' — the most valuable executive question.

tree.if: Your message is about a TREND or CHANGE over sequential time periods
tree.why: Time series show trajectory and inflection points.

tree.if: Your message is about RANKING or COMPARING discrete items
tree.why: Bars make magnitude differences visually obvious.

tree.if: Your message is about COMPOSITION or share of a total
tree.then: donut (<=6 segments) or stacked_bar (comparing composition across groups)
tree.why: Parts-of-whole charts show concentration and dominance.

tree.if: Your message is about a FLOW from sources to destinations
tree.why: Sankey diagrams show volume redistribution — perfect for supply chain rerouting.

tree.if: Your message is about a single KPI relative to a THRESHOLD
tree.why: Gauges create urgency around a critical metric.

tree.if: Your message is about RELATIONSHIP between two variables
tree.why: Scatter plots reveal whether two things are actually connected.

tree.if: Your message is about INTENSITY across two dimensions
tree.why: Heatmaps show where the hot spots are in a matrix.

tree.if: Your message is about CONVERSION or drop-off through stages
tree.why: Funnels show where volume is lost in a process.
When in doubt, a well-designed bar chart with clear labels is the safest choice.
